extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, policymakers, congressional staff, IP stakeholders (patent owners, defendants, universities, corporations)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of proposed statutory standards under the Patent Reform Act (e.g., priority/first‑to‑file, prior art, inventor oath/substitute statements, assignee filing, damages/royalty calculation, willfulness, prior user rights). Intended to guide how courts/USPTO and parties should apply these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑inventor‑to‑file system
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 creates a new “first‑inventor‑to‑file” system making the filing date most relevant in determining whether an application is patentable, moving the U.S. system closer to first‑to‑file systems used elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminates costly, complex interference proceedings (priority fights about who invented first) because priority is based on the first application. Creates a new administrative “derivation” proceeding to ensure the first person to file is actually a true inventor (so someone who has not invented something may not obtain a patent). Intended benefits: greater efficiency, greater certainty, reduced filing and litigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: One‑year grace period preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: The new system continues to provide inventors the benefit of the one‑year grace period: applicants’ own publication or disclosure occurring within one year prior to filing will not act as prior art against their applications; similarly, disclosure by others during that time based on information obtained (directly or indirectly) from the inventor will not constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee view: this one‑year grace period should continue to give U.S. applicants the time they need to prepare and file their applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art measured from filing date; geographic limits removed
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art will be measured from the filing date of the application and will typically include all art that publicly exists prior to the filing date. Prior art will no longer have geographic limitations: the “in this country” limitation as applied to “public use” and “on sale” is removed and the phrase “available to the public” is added to clarify scope. Prior art based on earlier‑filed U.S. applications is maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modifies prior art sections (compare current 35 U.S.C. §102(e) with new §102(a)(2)). The intent is clarity and broader, filing‑date‑based measurement of what is publicly available. The CREATE Act prior‑art exception for joint research activity is preserved and moved consistently into the renumbered statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute inventor’s statement in lieu of oath (Inventor’s oath/declaration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 115 is amended to allow a substitute statement to be submitted in lieu of an inventor’s oath where either the inventor is (i) unable to do so, or (ii) is both unwilling to do so and under an obligation to assign the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an error is discovered, the statement may later be corrected. A savings clause prevents an invalidity or unenforceability challenge based on failure to comply with these requirements, provided any error has been remedied. Willful false statements remain punishable under federal criminal law (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §1001). The change is intended to modernize filing procedures to facilitate assignee filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee and obligated assignee filing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 118 is amended to make it easier for an assignee to file a patent application: obligated assignees (entities to which an inventor is obligated to assign) may file applications; a person with a sufficient proprietary interest in the invention may file to preserve rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to reflect modern practice where many applications are filed by or assigned to corporate entities and to reduce difficulty locating every inventor’s signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge must determine damages domain and identify relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge is required to determine, from the liability phase of the trial and any additional hearings, whether the case falls within the “entire market value” domain, the “marketplace licensing” domain, or outside both those realms. The judge must also identify for the jury all, and only, the relevant factors in determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Envisions a more active, better‑documented role for district courts (with the aid of the parties) in giving juries guidance on appropriate law for calculating reasonable royalties. Aims to give judges and juries better guidance on how to calculate a reasonable royalty so awards reflect harm caused by infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire market value rule: predicate for application
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire market value rule may be applied if the patented invention’s contribution over the prior art is the predominant basis, and not just one of several bases, for the market demand of the infringing product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as a codification of existing law (Rite‑Hite v. Kelley) and to limit application of the entire market value rule to situations where the patented feature drives demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketplace licensing domain (use of comparable licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty may be based on other comparable, nonexclusive licenses of the patented invention if there has been a sufficient number of licenses to indicate a general marketplace recognition of the reasonableness of the licensing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee heard that existing licenses of the patent can be among the better indicators of an appropriate royalty when sufficient comparable license evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback: reasonable royalty must be attributable to specific contribution over prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If neither the entire market value rule nor marketplace licensing is applicable, the trier of fact must ensure the damages award accurately reflects the harm caused by the infringement; the jury is admonished to apply the reasonable royalty calculation only to the portion of the economic value of the infringing product or process properly attributable to the claimed invention’s specific contribution over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee intends “specific contribution over the prior art” to capture the ‘actual invention’ or the reason the patent was allowed. For combination inventions whose elements are individually in the prior art, contribution may include added function or enhanced value from the combination, if demonstrated. Language mandating a specific methodology (e.g., apportionment) was removed; instead the court shall exclude economic value properly attributable to prior art and other features or improvements (whether patented or not). The provision is aimed at ensuring damages reflect harm from the claimed invention, not unrelated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and scope of the Georgia‑Pacific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may consider (or direct a jury to consider) any of the 15 Georgia‑Pacific factors that may be relevant to a given damage calculation, as well as any other factors courts determine relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgia‑Pacific’s fifteen factors are non‑exclusive and tend to fall into three categories: (i) royalty rates people have been willing to pay for similar inventions; (ii) the significance of the patented invention to the product and market demand; and (iii) expert testimony as to value. Committee notes juries often lack sufficient guidance when presented with all 15 factors in a list; the judge’s role is to identify the relevant subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: No effect on non‑reasonable‑royalty damage awards (e.g., lost profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: These changes have no effect on damage awards not based on reasonable royalty calculations (for example, when lost profits is the appropriate remedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subsection preserves existing law and practice for lost profits and other non‑royalty remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness: judge determination and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness will be decided by the judge and only after finding that the patent was valid and infringed. Willfulness must be demonstrated by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to reduce unwarranted allegations of willfulness and unnecessary costly discovery. This replaces the common practice of pleading willfulness early and leaving it to a jury before validity/infringement is adjudicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness pleading and notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusive or boilerplate allegations no longer suffice for notice of infringement; the patent holder must allege acts of infringement sufficient to give the alleged infringer an objectively reasonable apprehension of suit, and must plead with particularity which products or processes allegedly infringe which claims of the patent, as well as the basis for such a belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to prevent pleading of willfulness based on conclusory letters or vague accusations; intended to curb abusive pleadings that impose discovery burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional grounds for finding willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Willfulness may be found if the infringer intentionally copied the patented invention with knowledge it was patented, or if the infringer continued to engage in infringing conduct after a court already found the party to be infringing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit bases for willfulness under the proposed statutory text (subparagraphs (e)(2)(B) and (e)(2)(C)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful good faith defense to willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged infringer can establish a good faith defense through reasonable reliance on the advice of counsel; evidence that the infringer sought to modify its conduct to avoid infringement once it had discovered the patent; or other evidence a court may find sufficient. The decision not to present evidence of advice of counsel is not relevant to a determination of willful infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a statutory safe harbor for reliance on counsel and conduct demonstrating good faith, reducing perverse incentives (e.g., to avoid patent searches) created by current willfulness doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights: affiliates and mandated study
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduced bill would have extended prior user rights broadly, but the adopted amendment limited the change to clarifying that “affiliates” of the user may also assert the defense (affiliates include those who caused or controlled the acts that were performed that give rise to the defense). The Act also instructs the USPTO Director to conduct and report a study with recommendations on prior user rights within two years of enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change narrows the scope of prior user rights amendment in response to stakeholder concerns (e.g., universities/tech transfer) while committing to a study to evaluate further action domestically and internationally.
